stem: Best guess: a U.S. corporation opens a sales office in France that loses money in its first year. If the office is a branch rather than a French subsidiary, what happens to the loss?

choices.explanation: That describes a subsidiary, a separate taxpayer.

choices.text: It is deducted on the U.S. return
choices.explanation: Correct. A branch is part of the U.S. corporation, so its loss flows into the U.S. return.

choices.text: It becomes a foreign tax credit
choices.explanation: A loss is a deduction, not a credit.

choices.text: It is disallowed by the U.S.
choices.explanation: Branch losses are deductible currently.

explanation: A branch's income and losses are part of the U.S. corporation's return.

stem: A U.S. corporation has worldwide taxable income of $1,000,000, including $300,000 of foreign-source taxable income, and U.S. tax before credits of $210,000. It paid $50,000 of foreign income tax. What foreign tax credit is allowed?

choices.explanation: That is the limit; the credit cannot exceed the foreign tax paid.
The credit is limited to U.S. tax on foreign-source income.
Correct. The limit is 210,000 × 300,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 63,000; foreign tax paid (50,000) is lower.
This multiplies the foreign tax by the foreign-source share.

explanation: Credit = lesser of foreign taxes paid or U.S. tax × foreign-source ÷ worldwide taxable income.

stem: A U.S. corporation receives interest on a loan to a French company and dividends from a U.S. corporation. How is each sourced?

choices.explanation: Correct. Interest and dividends are sourced by the residence of the payer.
Interest is sourced by the payer's residence, not the recipient's.
Dividends from a domestic corporation are U.S.-source.
Both are sourced by the payer; this reverses them.

explanation: Interest and dividend income are sourced by the residence of the payer.

stem: A U.S. engineer employed by a U.S. company spends three months working in Brazil on a client project and is paid $60,000 for that work by the U.S. company. Where is the $60,000 sourced?

choices.explanation: Compensation is sourced where the services are performed, not by the payer.

choices.text: Brazil, where the work was done
choices.explanation: Correct. Compensation for personal services is sourced where the services are performed.
The worker's residence does not determine the source of compensation.
The services were all performed in Brazil.

explanation: Personal services income is sourced where the services are performed.

stem: A U.S. manufacturer buys inventory in Mexico and resells it to customers in Canada, with title passing in Canada. Where is the income from the sales sourced?

choices.explanation: Purchased inventory is sourced where title passes, not by residence.
The place of purchase does not determine source.
Correct. Income from the sale of purchased inventory is sourced where title passes.
The payment location is irrelevant.

explanation: Purchased inventory: title-passage rule. Produced inventory: where the production occurs.

stem: A foreign corporation with no U.S. trade or business receives $100,000 of dividends from a U.S. corporation. No treaty applies. How is the income taxed?

choices.explanation: Net-basis tax at regular rates applies to effectively connected income, not passive FDAP income.

choices.text: It is exempt from U.S. tax
choices.explanation: U.S.-source FDAP income of a foreign person is taxable.

choices.text: It is taxed only when repatriated
choices.explanation: The tax is collected at the time of payment.
Correct. U.S.-source FDAP income is taxed at 30% of the gross amount, collected by withholding, absent a treaty.

explanation: FDAP income not connected with a U.S. business: 30% gross withholding (§§881, 1442), often reduced by treaty.

stem: A German company sells machines to U.S. customers. Which arrangement is most likely to create a U.S. permanent establishment under a typical treaty?

choices.text: A U.S. agent who signs its contracts
choices.explanation: Correct. A dependent agent who habitually concludes contracts on the company's behalf creates a permanent establishment.
Selling into the U.S. without a presence creates no permanent establishment.

choices.text: A U.S. warehouse used only for storage
choices.explanation: Storage alone is a preparatory or auxiliary activity.
An independent agent acting in the ordinary course of its business is not a permanent establishment.

explanation: A permanent establishment is a fixed place of business or a dependent agent that habitually concludes contracts; auxiliary activities are excluded.

stem: A U.S. corporation expects its new foreign operation to lose money for three years. Which structure lets it use those losses against U.S. income?

choices.explanation: A foreign subsidiary is a separate taxpayer; its losses stay abroad.
Correct. A branch is part of the U.S. corporation, so its losses reduce U.S. taxable income.
A CFC is a foreign subsidiary; its losses do not flow to the parent.

choices.text: Either structure; the choice is irrelevant
choices.explanation: Only the branch passes losses through.

explanation: Start-up losses favor a branch; later profits taxed at lower foreign rates may favor a subsidiary.

stem: Five unrelated U.S. corporations each own 11% of the voting stock of a foreign corporation; foreign persons own the rest. Is the foreign corporation a CFC?

choices.text: No — no single owner has control
choices.explanation: CFC status looks at all U.S. shareholders together.
The threshold is more than 50%.
Correct. Each owns at least 10%, so each is a U.S. shareholder; together they own 55%, more than 50%.

choices.text: Yes — any U.S. ownership makes it one
choices.explanation: Owners below 10% are not counted, and the total must exceed 50%.

explanation: CFC: more than 50% of vote or value owned by U.S. shareholders, each owning at least 10%.

stem: What is the main consequence for a U.S. shareholder of a CFC that earns Subpart F income?

choices.text: The CFC pays U.S. tax at 21% directly
choices.explanation: The U.S. shareholder, not the CFC, is taxed.

choices.text: The income is exempt until sold
choices.explanation: Subpart F income is taxed currently.
Withholding applies to FDAP paid to foreign persons.

choices.text: It is taxed on its share as earned
choices.explanation: Correct. Subpart F requires U.S. shareholders to include their pro rata share currently.

explanation: Subpart F (and GILTI) are anti-deferral regimes: U.S. shareholders include CFC income currently.

stem: A U.S. corporation has worldwide taxable income of $4,000,000, including $1,000,000 of foreign-source taxable income, and U.S. tax before credits of $840,000. It paid $300,000 of foreign tax. What is its excess foreign tax credit?

choices.explanation: That is the credit allowed, not the excess.
The foreign tax paid exceeds the limit.
This uses 25% of the foreign tax instead of the limit formula.

explanation: Excess credit = foreign taxes paid − FTC limit.

stem: A U.S. corporation has $900,000 of gross income: $600,000 U.S.-source and $300,000 foreign-source. It has $150,000 of expenses definitely related to the foreign income and $200,000 of general expenses apportioned by gross income. What is its foreign-source taxable income?

choices.explanation: This omits the apportioned share of general expenses.
This apportions half of the general expenses instead of one-third.
Deductions must be allocated and apportioned to foreign-source income.

explanation: Allocate definitely related expenses first, then apportion the rest on a reasonable basis.

stem: A U.S. corporation owns 30% of a foreign corporation (not a CFC) and receives a dividend paid out of the foreign corporation's foreign earnings. What deduction may apply?

choices.explanation: The 50% and 65% DRDs apply to dividends from domestic corporations.

choices.text: A foreign tax credit for all taxes
choices.explanation: A deduction, not a credit, is the key relief here; §245A dividends do not carry a deemed-paid credit.
Correct. §245A allows a 100% deduction for the foreign-source portion of dividends from a 10%-owned foreign corporation (holding period met).

choices.text: None; foreign dividends are fully taxed
choices.explanation: §245A provides a participation exemption for 10% corporate shareholders.

explanation: §245A: a 100% DRD for the foreign-source portion of dividends from specified 10%-owned foreign corporations.
